1.scope: On 2026-10-31, by the maintainer’s decisions of 2026-10-30 and 2026-10-31 and the corrections of a blind cross-family check, the first part of a machine-prepared, machine-audited candidate pack on the kinds of AI and their technical history was admitted: the documents it rests on, five persons, authorship, citation and reported-use records, attributed statements crediting persons, and dated statements of what texts say about systems, results and releases from 1955 to 2023, each recorded as its own text states it. Retrospective accounts are attributed and their dates labelled as claimed. All records are seeds; none is human-reviewed.

2.snapshotDescription: Dataset state before part 2 of the technical history admission (2026-10-31): the IDs it adds and the rows it changes as they were.
2.scope: On 2026-10-31 the second part of the technical history pack was admitted under schema 2.26: eleven families of methods and seven names used in the history of machine intelligence, each a concept with a criterion, the located texts that name each family or use each name, with the earliest located use where the recorded searches establish one and a withheld role where unread leads could decide it, and quoted defining statements. Earliest located never means first; order is not influence. By the maintainer’s decision of 2026-10-31 it also records attributed credits to works (schema 2.25), each the citing text’s claim, and three citations. All records are seeds; none is human-reviewed.

newClaims.subject: th-schwartz-1986-limits-of-ai
newClaims.statement: Schwartz’s report “The Limits of Artificial Intelligence” (March 1986) uses ‘superintelligences’ for artificial minds able to explore alternatives and act at a rate far exceeding human ability.

time.note: Date on the report’s cover (Technical Report #212, March 1986).

newClaims.qualification: Earliest located use by the recorded searches, found by the cross-family check (2026-10-30); not evidence of coinage. The plural noun meets the criterion. The text is read in OCR of a digitised copy, not in a page facsimile.

evidence.passage: artificial superintelligences able to explore significant mathematical, scientific, or engineering alternatives at a rate far exceeding human ability, or to generate plans and take action on them with equally overwhelming speed.
evidence.reason: Located by the cross-family check (item 2) and matched again in a direct retrieval at admission on 2026-10-31, whose SHA-256 equals the check’s.

newClaims.subject: th-nips-2007-deep-learning-workshop
newClaims.statement: The announcement page of the NIPS 2007 Deep Learning Workshop, in its revision of 12 October 2007, uses ‘deep learning’ for learning in deep architectures with multiple levels of non-linear operations, such as neural nets with many hidden layers.

time.note: Date of revision 1 in the page header, as an archive capture of 18 October 2007 shows it. The workshop itself was planned for 6 December 2007, a separate date.

newClaims.qualification: Earliest located use in the neural sense by the recorded searches, found by the cross-family check (2026-10-30); not evidence of coinage. The page was read only by the check, in an Internet Archive capture of 18 October 2007, which attests the wording by that date; this admission could not open the capture.

attested.note: Internet Archive capture of 18 October 2007, opened by the cross-family check.

evidence.locator: Workshop description, second and third sentences
evidence.passage: The page defines deep architectures as composed of multiple levels of non-linear operations, such as neural nets with many hidden layers, and says that the workshop is meant to bring together researchers interested in the question of deep learning.
evidence.reason: Read by the cross-family check (item 5) in the capture of 18 October 2007, which quotes the third sentence verbatim. This admission could not open the capture, so the passage is given as Selekoa’s paraphrase of the check’s reading, not as a quotation.

th-mark-1977-expert-systems.description: William S. Mark, “The Reformulation Approach to Building Expert Systems”. Proceedings of the Fifth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (Cambridge, MA), pp. 329–334 (published 1977). Known from the proceedings index only.

th-feigenbaum-1977-art-of-ai.name: The Art of Artificial Intelligence: I. Themes and case studies of knowledge engineering
th-feigenbaum-1977-art-of-ai.description: Edward A. Feigenbaum, “The Art of Artificial Intelligence: I. Themes and case studies of knowledge engineering”. Proceedings of the Fifth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (Cambridge, MA), pp. 1014–1028 (published 1977).

th-lighthill-1973-general-survey.name: Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey
th-lighthill-1973-general-survey.description: James Lighthill’s survey, dated July 1972, published by the Science Research Council in 1973 as Part I of “Artificial Intelligence: a paper symposium”. The preface reports that the Council discussed the report in September 1972 and decided to publish it.

th-kowalski-1974-predicate-logic.name: Predicate Logic as Programming Language
th-kowalski-1974-predicate-logic.description: Robert Kowalski, “Predicate Logic as Programming Language”. Information Processing 74 (IFIP Congress proceedings), North-Holland (published 1974). IFIP 74 congress, Stockholm, as recalled by the author in 1988 (date claimed by a later account or citation: August 1974).

th-kowalski-1988-early-years.name: The Early Years of Logic Programming
th-kowalski-1988-early-years.description: Robert A. Kowalski, “The Early Years of Logic Programming”. Communications of the ACM, January 1988 (pp. 38 onward) (published January 1988). Retrospective account by a participant.

th-colmerauer-roussel-1992-birth-of-prol.name: The birth of Prolog
th-colmerauer-roussel-1992-birth-of-prol.description: Alain Colmerauer and Philippe Roussel’s retrospective account of the origins of Prolog, read in an author-hosted copy whose title page is dated November 1992. That date is the copy’s dateline; no publication date of this expression was verified.

th-buchanan-shortliffe-1984-rule-based-e.name: Rule-Based Expert Systems: The MYCIN Experiments of the Stanford Heuristic Programming Project
th-buchanan-shortliffe-1984-rule-based-e.description: Bruce G. Buchanan (ed.) and Edward H. Shortliffe (ed.), “Rule-Based Expert Systems: The MYCIN Experiments of the Stanford Heuristic Programming Project”. Addison Wesley, Reading, MA (published 1984). Edited volume; chapter 1 read.

th-ibm-deep-blue-heritage.name: Deep Blue
th-ibm-deep-blue-heritage.description: IBM’s undated Heritage page on Deep Blue, its own later account of the system and of the 1996 and 1997 matches with Garry Kasparov. Read as served on 2026-10-29.

th-brants-2007.name: Large Language Models in Machine Translation
th-brants-2007.description: Thorsten Brants and others, “Large Language Models in Machine Translation”. EMNLP-CoNLL 2007 proceedings, pp. 858-867 (published June 2007). Authors affiliated as printed with Google, Inc.; n-gram (statistical) language models, not neural networks.

th-witteveen-2019.name: Paraphrasing with Large Language Models
th-witteveen-2019.description: Sam Witteveen and Martin Andrews, “Paraphrasing with Large Language Models”. WNGT 2019 workshop, Hong Kong (date as printed in the proceedings footer) (conference, 4 November 2019).

kp-neural-machine-translation-by-jointly.name: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
kp-neural-machine-translation-by-jointly.description: Dzmitry Bahdanau, KyungHyun Cho and Yoshua Bengio, “Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate”. arXiv:1409.0473v1 (submitted 1 September 2014).

kp-improving-language-understanding-by-g.name: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training
kp-improving-language-understanding-by-g.description: Alec Radford and others, “Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training”. Year given in a later citation (GPT-2 paper reference list) (date claimed by a later account or citation: 2018). Called GPT-1 in later usage; the paper itself names its model "our model" and the reference lists of later texts name it by title.

kp-bert-pre-training-deep-bidirectional-.name: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
kp-bert-pre-training-deep-bidirectional-.description: Jacob Devlin and others, “BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding”. arXiv:1810.04805v1 (submitted 11 October 2018).

kp-language-models-unsupervised-multitas.name: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
kp-language-models-unsupervised-multitas.description: Alec Radford and others, “Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners”. Year given in a later citation (GPT-3 paper reference list) (date claimed by a later account or citation: 2019).

kp-language-models-few-shot-learners-202.name: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
kp-language-models-few-shot-learners-202.description: Tom B. Brown and et al., “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners”. arXiv:2005.14165v1 (submitted 28 May 2020).

kp-opportunities-risks-foundation-models.name: On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models
kp-opportunities-risks-foundation-models.description: Rishi Bommasani and et al., “On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models”. arXiv:2108.07258v1 (submitted 16 August 2021).

th-openai-2022-introducing-chatgpt.name: Introducing ChatGPT
th-openai-2022-introducing-chatgpt.description: OpenAI, “Introducing ChatGPT”. Month given in a later citation (GPT-4 system card reference [101]) (date claimed by a later account or citation: November 2022).

th-zhao-2023-llm-survey.name: A Survey of Large Language Models
th-zhao-2023-llm-survey.description: Wayne Xin Zhao and others, “A Survey of Large Language Models”. arXiv:2303.18223v1 (submitted 31 March 2023). A survey: secondary for the history it recounts; primary for its own definitions.

th-mnih-2013-atari.name: Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning
th-mnih-2013-atari.description: Volodymyr Mnih and others, “Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning”. arXiv:1312.5602v1 (submitted 19 December 2013). Affiliation printed as DeepMind Technologies.

kp-human-level-control-through-deep-2015.name: Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning
kp-human-level-control-through-deep-2015.description: Volodymyr Mnih and others, “Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning”. Nature 518, 529-533 (online publication) (published 25 February 2015).

kp-mastering-game-go-deep-neural-2016.name: Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search
kp-mastering-game-go-deep-neural-2016.description: David Silver and others, “Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search”. Nature 529, 484-489 (online publication) (published 27 January 2016).

th-hassabis-2016-seoul.name: What we learned in Seoul with AlphaGo
th-hassabis-2016-seoul.description: Demis Hassabis, “What we learned in Seoul with AlphaGo”. Post date as displayed on blog.google (announced 16 March 2016). Byline: Demis Hassabis, CEO and Co-Founder, DeepMind. Current page; not an authenticated 2016 capture.

th-lyashenko-2013-contact.name: On the validity of the method of reduction of dimensionality: area of contact, average interfacial separation and contact stiffness
th-lyashenko-2013-contact.description: I.A. Lyashenko, Lars Pastewka and Bo N. J. Persson, “On the validity of the method of reduction of dimensionality: area of contact, average interfacial separation and contact stiffness”. arXiv:1303.0965v1 (submitted 5 March 2013).

th-hu-turin-brown-1996.name: Language Modeling with Stochastic Automata
th-hu-turin-brown-1996.description: Jianying Hu, William Turin and Michael K. Brown, “Language Modeling with Stochastic Automata”. ICSLP 96, Philadelphia, 3–6 October 1996 (conference, October 1996).

th-schwartz-1986-limits-of-ai.name: The Limits of Artificial Intelligence
th-schwartz-1986-limits-of-ai.description: Jacob T. Schwartz’s article for the Encyclopedia of Artificial Intelligence, issued as Technical Report #212 of the Department of Computer Science, Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, New York University, dated March 1986 on its cover. Read in the Internet Archive’s OCR text of a digitised library copy, not in a page facsimile.

th-nips-2007-deep-learning-workshop.name: Deep Learning Workshop: Foundations and Future Directions
th-nips-2007-deep-learning-workshop.description: The announcement page of a workshop at NIPS 2007, organised by Yoshua Bengio, Yann LeCun, Ruslan Salakhutdinov and Hugo Larochelle, on the LISA laboratory wiki of the Université de Montréal. An Internet Archive capture of 18 October 2007 shows revision 1 of the page, dated 12 October 2007; the workshop was planned for 6 December 2007.

mark-avrum-gubrud.name: Mark Avrum Gubrud
mark-avrum-gubrud.description: Byline of a 1997 paper for the Fifth Foresight Conference on Molecular Nanotechnology, which prints his affiliation then as the Center for Superconductivity Research, University of Maryland. No later affiliation or role is recorded.

ben-goertzel.name: Ben Goertzel
ben-goertzel.description: Author of a 2011 blog post on the term “AGI” and of a 2002 SL4 mailing-list message. No affiliation or role is recorded.

edward-feigenbaum.name: Edward A. Feigenbaum
edward-feigenbaum.description: Author of “The Art of Artificial Intelligence” (IJCAI 1977). Recorded here as named in attributed statements about the term “knowledge engineering”; no affiliation or role is recorded.

philippe-roussel.name: Philippe Roussel
philippe-roussel.description: Co-author of “The birth of Prolog” (dated November 1992). Recorded here as named in attributed statements about the name Prolog; no affiliation or role is recorded.

alain-colmerauer.name: Alain Colmerauer
alain-colmerauer.description: Co-author of “The birth of Prolog” (dated November 1992). Recorded here as named in an attributed statement about the origins of Prolog; no affiliation or role is recorded.

th-term-agi.name: 'artificial general intelligence' / 'AGI'
th-term-agi.description: A name used in the history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the uses that meet it. Its records say which located texts use the name; none says where the name began.

naming.criterion: A passage uses the words 'artificial general intelligence' (or the abbreviation 'AGI' for them) as a name for machine intelligence of general, broadly human-level or greater scope; 'general intelligence' alone, 'strong AI' and 'general artificial intelligence' do not meet it.

th-term-superintelligence.name: 'superintelligence'
th-term-superintelligence.description: A name used in the history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the uses that meet it. Its records say which located texts use the name; none says where the name began.

naming.criterion: A passage uses the noun 'superintelligence' (or 'super-intelligence') for an intellect, machine or mind that greatly exceeds human intelligence, in the context of artificial or post-human minds; a use for exceptionally gifted humans, aliens or a deity is other-sense.

th-term-artificial-intelligence.name: 'artificial intelligence'
th-term-artificial-intelligence.description: A name used in the history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the uses that meet it. Its records say which located texts use the name; none says where the name began.

naming.criterion: A passage uses 'artificial intelligence' as the name of a field of study or of the capability of machines to perform tasks taken to require intelligence.

th-fam-connectionism.name: Connectionism and neural networks
th-fam-connectionism.description: A family of methods in the technical history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the passages that name or describe it. Its records say which located texts name and describe it; none says where it began.

naming.criterion: A passage names, with one of the listed names, networks of interconnected neuron-like units (natural or artificial) as a model of computation, memory or learning; "nervous nets" and "nets of neurons" in a purely physiological description are recorded as descriptions, not as naming.

withheld.reason: Titles before 1955 found by an index search name nets of neurons as formal models (Pitts 1942; Landahl 1944; Landahl and Runge 1946; Studley 1949; Rapoport 1950) and were not read. The cross-family check located wording in McCulloch and Pitts (1943), read in a 2008 reprint whose original date was not independently verified, with a singular base-case wording that needs a narrow qualification. The original journal facsimile and the 1942 Pitts paper decide the role.

th-fam-deep-learning.name: Deep learning
th-fam-deep-learning.description: A family of methods in the technical history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the passages that name or describe it. Its records say which located texts name and describe it; none says where it began.

naming.criterion: A passage describes learning in models with many layers of learned representations (multi-layer neural networks or similar architectures). Its naming records are those of the term ‘deep learning’ in the neural-network sense.

th-term-deep-learning.name: 'deep learning' (neural networks)
th-term-deep-learning.description: A name used in the history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the uses that meet it. Its records say which located texts use the name; none says where the name began.

naming.criterion: The string "deep learning" (or "Deep Learning") used for learning in neural networks or comparable multi-layer architectures with several layers of learned representation; uses for depth of search, for conflict-set learning in constraint satisfaction, or for students' approaches to study are other senses.

th-term-machine-learning.name: 'machine learning'
th-term-machine-learning.description: A name used in the history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the uses that meet it. Its records say which located texts use the name; none says where the name began.

naming.criterion: A passage uses "machine learning" (or the adjectival "machine-learning") for learning by computing machines or programs, as a name for a subject, method or field; uses for learning to operate a machine are another sense.

withheld.reason: Campaigne’s paper for the Western Joint Computer Conference (3–5 March 1959) is known only from its title as indexed; its body was not read (the ACM Digital Library refused), so its sense is open, and earlier texts were not checked. The earliest text read in full and dated is Samuel’s IBM Journal paper (July 1959, read in an unmarked later reprint whose date the publisher’s metadata confirms), a candidate if Campaigne’s text does not meet the criterion.

th-fam-probabilistic.name: Probabilistic and Bayesian methods
th-fam-probabilistic.description: A family of methods in the technical history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the passages that name or describe it. Its records say which located texts name and describe it; none says where it began.

naming.criterion: A passage names an approach to machine inference, decision or reasoning as Bayesian or probabilistic (for example "Bayes nets", "Bayesian networks", "Bayes inference"); for a definition, it states what the approach does with probabilities.

th-fam-evolutionary.name: Evolutionary computation
th-fam-evolutionary.description: A family of methods in the technical history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the passages that name or describe it. Its records say which located texts name and describe it; none says where it began.

naming.criterion: A passage names, as a method of computation or optimisation, a procedure modelled on biological evolution (variation and selection in a population), under a name such as evolutionary programming, evolution strategy, genetic algorithm, simulated evolution or evolutionary computation.

withheld.reason: Koza (1990) cites Fogel, Owens and Walsh, Artificial Intelligence through Simulated Evolution (1966), which was not read; the cross-family check found only an undated publisher announcement of that book, which does not date its own wording. Burgin’s 1973 title is known only from an index, and the 1958–1967 texts cited for the family (Friedberg, Bremermann, Rechenberg, Holland 1962) were not reached.

th-fam-statistical-learning.name: Statistical learning and support-vector machines
th-fam-statistical-learning.description: A family of methods in the technical history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the passages that name or describe it. Its records say which located texts name and describe it; none says where it began.

naming.criterion: A passage names support-vector methods or statistical learning theory (or, for learning theory, gives a formal account of what can be learned from examples drawn from a distribution).

withheld.reason: Valiant’s journal article of November 1984, read, is a dated candidate under the criterion’s learning-theory clause, as the cross-family check found; it does not use the words “statistical learning”. Earlier work on uniform convergence (Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1960s–1970s) and Boser, Guyon and Vapnik (1992, “optimal margin classifiers”) were not read; the criterion and these leads need reconciling before a headline.

th-fam-neurosymbolic.name: Hybrid and neurosymbolic approaches
th-fam-neurosymbolic.description: A family of methods in the technical history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the passages that name or describe it. Its records say which located texts name and describe it; none says where it began.

naming.criterion: A passage names an approach that combines neural-network (connectionist) learning with symbolic knowledge or reasoning, as "hybrid", "neuro-symbolic", "neural-symbolic" or "neurosymbolic".

withheld.reason: Towell, Shavlik and Noordewier (AAAI 1990) is a dated candidate the cross-family check located. Titles of 1988–1991 found by an index search name hybrid symbolic and connectionist models (Nenov and Dyer 1988; Hendler 1989; Wermter and Lehnert 1989; Kasabov 1990; Rose and Belew 1991) and were not read or were refused.

th-fam-symbolic-ai.name: Symbolic AI and expert systems
th-fam-symbolic-ai.description: A family of methods in the technical history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the passages that name or describe it. Its records say which located texts name and describe it; none says where it began.

naming.criterion: A passage names, by one of the usual names listed, the approach of building intelligent programs from explicitly represented symbols, rules or encoded expert knowledge manipulated by inference; for a definition, it says what such a system or practice is.

withheld.reason: Feigenbaum’s 1977 paper, read in full, is a dated candidate. An earlier lead is Michie’s 1973 paper, known to the cross-family check only from its title and abstract in index metadata; Malhotra’s February 1975 thesis (cited, not read) and the 1969–1974 Stanford reports were not read.

th-fam-search-planning.name: Search and planning
th-fam-search-planning.description: A family of methods in the technical history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the passages that name or describe it. Its records say which located texts name and describe it; none says where it began.

naming.criterion: A passage names search (the exploration of a space of possible solutions, usually guided by heuristics) or planning (constructing a sequence of actions or steps to reach a goal) as a method, technique or area of machine problem solving; for a definition, it says what the method is.

withheld.reason: The revised summary of the General Problem Solver report (stamped 9 February 1959) is a dated candidate; its original cover date (30 December 1958) does not date the revised wording. Simon and Newell’s 1958 Operations Research article, the full text of the 1956 Logic Theory Machine report and the 1956–1957 Logic Theory papers were not read for this role.

th-fam-logic-programming.name: Logic programming
th-fam-logic-programming.description: A family of methods in the technical history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the passages that name or describe it. Its records say which located texts name and describe it; none says where it began.

naming.criterion: A passage names, as "logic programming" or a close variant, the use of logical sentences (such as Horn clauses) as programs executed by a proof procedure; for a definition, it says what logic programming is.
terms: predicate logic as a programming language

th-fam-transformers-llm.name: Transformers and large language models
th-fam-transformers-llm.description: A family of methods in the technical history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the passages that name or describe it. Its records say which located texts name and describe it; none says where it began.

naming.criterion: A passage names the family when it names the Transformer architecture (a sequence model built on attention without recurrence) or the class of language models built on it; it describes the family when it states what that architecture or class consists of.

th-term-large-language-model.name: 'large language model'
th-term-large-language-model.description: A name used in the history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the uses that meet it. Its records say which located texts use the name; none says where the name began.

naming.criterion: The phrase "large language model(s)" names a language model (a probability model over word sequences, statistical or neural) that the passage distinguishes by its scale of training data or parameters; uses of "large" for vocabulary size, corpus size alone or the model of a large language class are other senses.

th-term-foundation-model.name: 'foundation model'
th-term-foundation-model.description: A name used in the history of machine intelligence, recorded with a criterion for the uses that meet it. Its records say which located texts use the name; none says where the name began.

naming.criterion: The phrase "foundation model(s)" names a machine-learning model trained on broad data and adapted to many downstream tasks; engineering uses (an elastic or soil foundation model) and "foundational model" are other senses.
